title: Onion Bhaji
subtitle: Crisp gram-flour fritters with sliced onion and spices
excerpt: The classic Indian-British starter: sliced onion in a spiced gram-flour batter, deep-fried until golden and crisp. The trick is the batter consistency and oil temperature. Best eaten straight from the oil.

recipe.sourceNotes: Bhaji or pakora in the Indian tradition refers to any vegetable coated in a spiced gram-flour batter and fried. The onion version became among the most popular Indian-British restaurant starters by the 1970s, often served with a mint chutney. In India the dish varies considerably by region; the British version tends to be a looser, lacy fritter rather than the compact, dense version sometimes found in different parts of the subcontinent.

recipeTools.notes: Deep pan for frying, or deep-fat fryer.

content.text: The batter should be thick enough to coat the onion strands but not so thick that the centre of the bhaji is raw when the outside is golden. Salt the onion first and leave it for 10 minutes; it will release water that helps bind the batter. Fry at 170 to 175 C. Too hot and the outside burns before the inside cooks; too cool and the bhajis are greasy rather than crisp.
Put the sliced onion in a bowl with the salt. Mix well and leave for 10 minutes. The onion will release water. Squeeze the onion firmly with your hands and leave the water in the bowl.

Add the gram flour, ginger, chilli, cumin seeds, ground coriander, turmeric, chilli powder, and fresh coriander to the onion. Mix well. Add cold water a tablespoon at a time until the batter just binds the onion. It should be thick and sticky, not pourable.

Heat the oil to 170 C in a deep pan. Carefully lower heaped tablespoons of the onion mixture into the oil. Fry for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and crisp. Cook in batches and do not crowd the pan. Drain on kitchen paper.
Serve immediately with mint chutney or yoghurt and sliced green chilli on the side.
